1.pericope_label: Son of man, set thy face against mount Seir, and prophesy against it
debates: Whether Edom stands for more than the historical nation
How many destructions of Idumea are foretold
How the two chapters are related
outliers: Ellicott and Gill read Edom as representative of the hostility of the world to the covenant people, while Clarke keeps to the historical bondage of the Edomites
Clarke reports the opinion of Calmet that two destructions are foretold, one by Nebuchadnezzar and another by the Jews after their return
Keil and Delitzsch hold this chapter and the next form one connected prophecy, the promise to the mountains of Israel being the obverse of the threat against the mountains of Seir
Gill asks how the prophet could address a people he was not among, and answers by ambassadors at Babylon or by letter
themes: A hereditary malice traced to a quarrel over the birthright and the blessing
An ancestor reconciled whose posterity never was
Children more apt to imitate the vices than the virtues of their parents
The land fixed between the Dead Sea and the Elanitic Gulf

5.pericope_label: Because thou hast had a perpetual hatred, and hast shed the blood of the children of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity
debates: How the charge should be rendered
What the time of their calamity refers to
Whether the hatred of Edom differs in kind from that of its neighbours
outliers: Ellicott holds that blood is not in the original and the clause should read that they scattered the children of Israel, the verb meaning literally to pour out

Ellicott fixes the calamity as the overthrow of Jerusalem, both the great calamity and the moment when their iniquity had an end; Wesley reads the phrase of the punishment that brought them to final ruin
Ellicott holds the hatred of Edom deeper than that of the other neighbours because coeval with its first ancestor
themes: A play on the name of Edom, that they should be made blood, the name meaning red
A conqueror whose head was thrown into a vessel of blood and bidden satisfy himself
Carriers grown rich on the trade between India and the East and Egypt
To afflict the afflicted called scarcely of man

10.pericope_label: Because thou hast said, These two nations and these two countries shall be mine, and we will possess it; whereas the LORD was there
debates: How wide the rejoicing of the whole earth is
Whether the words were blasphemies or reproaches
outliers: Gill allows either Idumea together with Israel, or the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah, and prefers the latter; Clarke and Ellicott take the two kingdoms without hesitation

Ellicott allows that Hebrew usage would bear the whole land of Israel but prefers the whole earth, since the thought is not confined to Edom; Wesley reads the countries round about and Clarke the land rejoicing in the restoration of the Jews
Ellicott would render blasphemies as reproaches, which became constructively blasphemies, and warns against pushing the meaning further than was intended
Clarke suggests the time of the desolation is probably that of the Maccabees
themes: A claim of title for want of other heirs, standing next in the entail
Troubles of the church drawing out more brutish malice than one would have thought of
A rage inflamed that needed no spur
A man said to make his own temporal good or evil by what he does to others
